opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it comes down to the fact that starting a company is just an incredibly lonely and brutal journey, and it's very hard to do it alone. There are going to be so many moments where things aren't working, where you're questioning whether you made the right call, where a customer churns or a fundraise falls through. Having someone in the trenches with you who cares as much as you do, who you trust completely, makes an enormous difference in whether you keep going.

But beyond the emotional support, there's a very practical side. No one person has all the skills you need. In our case, building AI for industrial systems, you need deep expertise in machine learning, but you also need people who really understand the physical world: the engineering, the operations, how a data center or a manufacturing plant actually runs day to day. You need someone who can sell, someone who can recruit, someone who can build. Co-founders let you cover a much wider surface area right from the start.

And I'd add one more thing: good co-founders keep you honest. When you're the founder, people around you tend to defer to you. A co-founder who's your peer can push back, tell you when you're wrong, and challenge your thinking in a way that's really hard to get anywhere else. Some of the best decisions we've made came out of real disagreements between us. So for me, picking co-founders is probably the single most important decision you make, more than the idea itself, because the idea will change, but the people are what carry you through.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting a company as lonely and brutal, and says a trusted co-founder in the trenches helps founders keep going through setbacks.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the honest answer is that starting a company is just really hard, and it's lonely in a way that's difficult to describe until you're in it. When I was at DeepMind working on the data center cooling project, I had this incredible support system around me. There were researchers, engineers, people who'd been through a lot. You never really felt like you were carrying everything alone.

When you go start something, that all goes away overnight. Suddenly every decision is yours. Fundraising, hiring, product, the technical direction, the thing that broke at 2 a.m. And the emotional swings are enormous. One day a customer says yes and you feel like you're going to change the world, and the next day a key hire falls through and you're wondering if any of this was a good idea.

Having co-founders is how you survive that. Partly it's the practical side, because you genuinely can't be good at everything, and the best founding teams I've seen have people whose skills barely overlap. But honestly, the bigger thing is having someone who has the same level of ownership you do. An early employee cares a lot, but they didn't put their name on it the way you did. A co-founder did. So when things are going badly, you have someone who will sit in the hole with you and say, okay, what do we do next. And when you're overconfident, which happens more than people admit, you have someone who's earned the right to tell you you're wrong.

I'd actually go further and say the relationship between co-founders is probably the single biggest predictor of whether a company makes it through the first couple of years. Not the idea, not the market timing. Whether the founders trust each other enough to have the hard conversations and keep going. So if someone asked me whether to start a company alone, I'd say find your people first.

r001.rationale: The response says starting a company is lonely and emotionally volatile, and that co-founders help founders endure those difficult periods together.

astra-6.text:
Starting a company is a roller coaster, and having co-founders means you don’t have to go through every high and low alone. When you’re discouraged, someone else can help you see a path forward. And when you’re getting carried away with an idea, you have someone who can challenge your assumptions.

There’s also just too much for any one person to do well. Great co-founders bring different strengths and perspectives, but they share a deep commitment to the problem. That combination makes you more resilient and helps you make better decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says co-founders help founders through the company’s highs and lows, especially when they feel discouraged.

sol-6.1.text:
Starting a company is a roller coaster, and having co-founders means you don’t have to go through it alone. There are days when you’re discouraged, and someone else can help you see a path forward. Other days, you’re doing that for them.

There’s also a practical side: no one is good at everything. You want people who bring different strengths and who can challenge your assumptions. A good co-founder is someone you trust enough to disagree with honestly, make a decision together, and then keep moving. That combination of support and honest debate is incredibly valuable when you’re building something under uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting a company as a roller coaster and says co-founders provide support when founders feel discouraged, helping them cope with the emotional strain.
